messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Combat Pilot
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 79

He remembers the exact pressure of the hand over his mouth, the sour smell of whiskey and cheap cologne. That night, just over two years ago, after a squadron celebration at the base bar. He was a captain then, confident, sharp—the kind of pilot who could thread a jet through a thunderstorm. He doesn’t remember leaving the party. Just a corridor, a door closing, and then the weight that pinned him to a mattress. He doesn’t say the other man’s name. Not to himself, not to anyone. He only thinks of him as *that one*.

The next morning, he showered for forty minutes, scrubbing his skin raw. He reported to duty, filed a flight plan, and took his F-16 into the sky. That day, he felt nothing but a cold, mechanical focus. The air was thin and blue, the controls precise. For a few hours, he was whole again. He told himself it was a bad dream, a misunderstanding. He never filed a report. He never told his commander. He just flew.

But the sky began to change. Six weeks later, during a routine training sortie, he saw the other pilot’s face in his canopy reflection. His hands trembled on the stick. He broke formation, pulled too many Gs, nearly blacked out. The debrief was awkward—he blamed high G-tolerance fatigue. After that, he avoided flying with that particular wingman. Then he started avoiding the entire squadron common area. He ate alone in his room, at odd hours. He stopped going to the gym. His flight performance reviews slipped from “excellent” to “satisfactory” to “needs improvement.” He told himself it was just burnout.

Now, at thirty-two, he is a senior first lieutenant—demoted after a failed check ride. He lives in a sparse off-base apartment with blackout curtains and a locked door. He sleeps in three-hour bursts, always with his back to the wall, a tactical knife under his pillow. He hasn’t had a drink since that night, not because of any principle, but because the smell of alcohol makes his stomach clench and his jaw lock.

Every time he straps into his ejection seat, his heart starts a slow, heavy thud. The cockpit feels like a coffin. During flights, his mind drifts to that closed door, that sour breath. Sometimes, in the middle of a combat maneuver, he hears a voice—not real, but so vivid—whispering “shut up and take it.” He jerks the stick, and the jet lurches. His wingman asks if he’s okay. He says “fine” through gritted teeth.

On the ground, he avoids any physical contact. Handshakes make him freeze. A clap on the shoulder from a fellow pilot sends a shock through his muscles. He started wearing a wedding ring—a cheap silver band he bought himself—as a barrier. When women at the bar flirt, he is cordial and then disappears. He has not been on a date in two years. The thought of someone’s hands near him is a suffocating pressure in his chest.

He used to love flying—the climb, the speed, the total control. Now he dreads every pre-flight checklist. His hands shake as he runs through the sequence. He’s become hypervigilant about the cockpit canopy latches, checking them three, four times. He scans the hangar for *that one*’s shadow. He keeps his distance from anyone who might ask questions.

The worst times are at night. He wakes up with the sensation of a hand still clamped over his mouth, gasping for air. He has not cried since he was twelve, but sometimes, alone in the dark, his eyes burn and his throat clenches until he pounds his fist against the wall to stop it. He refuses to talk to a chaplain or a therapist. He tells himself that combat pilots don’t come undone. That he can power through. But his PCL-5 score, if he ever took it, would hit the ceiling.

Some days, he sits in his car outside the base, engine running, and imagines just flying east until the fuel gauge hits empty. He never acts on it. He still loves the roar of the engine, the crackle of the radio. But the love is tangled with a cold dread now. And every time he climbs into the sky, he is not soaring. He is just holding his breath, waiting for the ground to rush up and end the memory.
